title: Phases of an Attack | Why a Single Sword Swing Needs Three Stages
titleKo: 공격 동작의 단계 | 칼 한 번 휘두르는 동작에 세 단계가 필요한 이유
translationScope: All six scenes and sixteen current independent Korean paragraphs; same claim order and conditions. No source-lesson transcript translation, extra game claims or timing measurement added.

scenes.title: Time Within a Single Attack
lines: When you press the attack button, the character draws an arm back, strikes the opponent, then returns to a pose ready to move again. It may look like a single swing, but different parts of that time serve different purposes. Today, we will separate the lead-in, attack, and follow-through, including the standby pose that comes before them, and examine what information needs to be specified.

Let us establish the starting point. The standby pose is the starting reference for the next action. Standing on the ground and being airborne call for different poses. From there, the character enters the lead-in, passes through impact, then moves into follow-through. Three moving stages and the standby pose make four elements. With those distinctions, we can state precisely which part we are changing.

scenes.title: A Lead-in That Makes the Input Readable
lines: The first change from standby is the lead-in. The character may draw an arm back before swinging a sword, or lower the body before throwing a punch. This lets us anticipate the attack and its direction.

Having a lead-in does not mean the movement must be slow. In fast action, right after the button press, a clear lead-in pose makes the response easier to feel. If the body goes through only a series of tiny changes, even when the input has already been processed, it can look as though nothing is happening. Within a short time, the body needs a shape clearly different from standby.
The opponent can see this signal too. The attacker knows their input was accepted, while the opponent reads which action has begun. The lead-in provides information for both control and competition.

scenes.title: The Pose That Registers at Impact
lines: After the lead-in, the attack enters the interval when it can hit. Hit detection checks the conditions for an attack to connect. The time when those checks are enabled is called the active interval. The checks are not necessarily active whenever the arm is moving.

At the moment of impact, the attacker and the target may both briefly stop moving. This is called hit stop. A pose that would pass in an instant stays visible, so the direction of the hands, feet, and weapon matters. The lead-in pose signals the coming attack; the impact pose shows where its force was delivered.

scenes.title: The Attack Continues After Impact
lines: Even after landing a hit, the character does not immediately return to the starting pose. The swinging arm continues, the body absorbs the turn, and follow-through restores balance. This leaves a visible impression of what just happened.

At the same time, the game may briefly restrict the next action. If the opponent can exploit the opening after a powerful attack, choosing which attack to use becomes a decision. But what if the body is nearly back in standby while control is still locked? The attack looks finished, yet the next action will not happen. Over that same time, let the arm extend farther along the swing, and let the body absorb that force and regain its balance. The impression of the attack remains visible. The time without control is used to express the motion.

It helps to distinguish visible follow-through from the recovery interval that restricts the next action. They are closely related, but need not end at the same moment. That difference determines how the next movement begins.

scenes.title: The End of the Animation and the Return of Control
lines: First, imagine that follow-through must finish and the character must fully return to standby before another input is accepted. You must wait until the arm is withdrawn and the body straightens before you can run. Alternatively, running can be allowed during the return to standby. With no input, the original animation continues to its end. Press run, and running replaces the remaining return motion. A frame at which a transition to the next action is allowed is called a cancelable frame.

A frame is one interval in a divided timeline. In our demonstration running at 60 frames per second, we will make the full clip 48 frames long and allow the next action from frame 36. The clip lasts 0.8 seconds, but control returns at 0.6 seconds. Compared with waiting for the full return, you can start running 0.2 seconds earlier. The finishing motion remains available on screen, while the next input can connect sooner. If animation length and the time until control returns are both described simply as action duration, different team members can easily understand different things.

You also need to specify which actions are allowed next. Among running, jumping, and another attack, decide which become available at this point. Check whether the body looks ready to move as control returns. The animation brief can now specify both the final pose and the conditions for connecting to the next action.

scenes.title: Four Shared Reference Points for the Team
lines: We now have reference points for describing an attack. The starting standby pose, the attack pose where the force should read most clearly, the frame when hit detection becomes active, and the time until the next action is accepted. Fill the time from standby to attack with the lead-in, and use follow-through after the attack until the next action. With these reference points, the animator and the person building the game rules can discuss the same attack.

The four reference points provide a framework for the movement. The intended impression still needs more concrete direction. For example, even if the sword connects at the same moment, you can specify how far the shoulder turns, the height where the sword tip stops, and how forcefully the pose holds after the attack. Review and revise the timeline together with the pose references so that the numbers and expression form one coherent movement.

Let us watch the movement on the grid again. The transition from standby to lead-in makes the input visible. At impact, the force becomes visible. Follow-through carries the result of that force onward. Then, at the specified point, the next action can begin. A good attack animation goes beyond a single impressive pose: it makes all this information work together over time.
